The sky looks blue because of a process called **Rayleigh scattering**.

Sunlight may look white, but it’s actually made up of many colors. When that light enters Earth’s atmosphere, it collides with tiny molecules of air. Those molecules scatter the light in different directions, but they don’t do it equally for every color.

Shorter wavelengths of light—like **blue and violet**—are scattered much more strongly than longer wavelengths like red or orange. Because blue light gets scattered all over the sky, it reaches your eyes from many directions. That’s why the daytime sky appears blue.

A small extra detail: violet light is scattered even more than blue, but the sky doesn’t look violet to us. That’s partly because human eyes are less sensitive to violet, and partly because some of it is absorbed before it reaches the ground.

So the short version is: **air molecules scatter sunlight, and blue light is scattered the most, making the sky look blue.**

Ice floats on water because it is less dense than liquid water. The reason comes down to how water molecules arrange themselves when they freeze.

Water is subject to hydrogen bonding, which means the molecules are attracted to each other in a specific way. In liquid water, those attractions are constantly breaking and reforming, and the molecules are packed relatively closely together. When the temperature drops enough for the water to freeze, the molecules settle into a more ordered crystalline structure. That structure forces the molecules to hold more space between them than they do in the liquid state.

Because the same amount of matter takes up more space as ice than as liquid water, ice has a lower density. Since less dense materials float on denser ones, ice rises to the surface and stays there.

This is a bit unusual for a solid. Most substances are denser when solid than when liquid, but water is one of the exceptions. That unusual property comes directly from the way its molecules organize during freezing.

The floating of ice has practical consequences, too. A layer of ice on the surface of a lake or pond helps insulate the water below, so the deeper water stays liquid longer. That is one reason many fish and other aquatic organisms can survive cold winters.

So the short version is: water expands when it freezes, and that expansion makes ice less dense than water, which is why ice floats.

Bread rises because of a combination of chemistry and physics, driven mainly by yeast. When flour, water, salt, and yeast are mixed into dough, the yeast begins to feed on the sugars present in the flour. As it metabolizes those sugars, it produces carbon dioxide gas and a small amount of alcohol. Those gas bubbles are the key reason the dough expands.

The carbon dioxide doesn’t simply escape into the air. Instead, it gets trapped inside the dough by a network of proteins called gluten, which forms when wheat flour is hydrated and worked. This elastic network acts like a stretchy scaffold, holding the gas in place while allowing the dough to expand. As more gas is produced, the bubbles grow and multiply, lifting the dough upward and outward.

The rising process usually happens in stages. The first rise, often called bulk fermentation, lets the yeast generate enough gas to create a lighter structure. After shaping, the dough rises again during proofing, which helps develop texture and flavor. Finally, when the loaf goes into the oven, the heat causes the remaining gases and moisture to expand even more, producing an extra burst of rise known as oven spring. At the same time, the crust sets and the crumb firms up.

So in simple terms, bread rises because yeast turns sugar into gas, and the dough’s gluten traps that gas until heat finishes the job. The result is a loaf with an airy structure instead of a dense one.

The Moon shows phases because of the way sunlight hits it and because it orbits Earth.

The Moon does not make its own light. What we see is sunlight reflecting off its surface. As the Moon moves around Earth during its roughly 29.5-day cycle, the amount of that lit side facing us changes. That changing view is what creates the phases.

- **New Moon:** The Moon is between Earth and the Sun, so the side facing us is dark.
- **First Quarter:** We see about half the Moon lit up.
- **Full Moon:** Earth is roughly between the Sun and Moon, so the entire visible side is illuminated.
- **Last Quarter:** Again about half is lit, but on the opposite side from the first quarter.

After that, the Moon appears to shrink back toward new moon, and the cycle repeats.

Even if a metal object and a wooden object are both at exactly the same temperature, they do not feel the same when you touch them. Metal is a very good thermal conductor. When you touch it, heat leaves your skin quickly and spreads through the metal surface and interior. Because the metal can carry that heat away efficiently, the spot you are touching stays relatively cool, and your hand keeps losing heat at a rapid rate. Your nervous system interprets that rapid heat loss as “cold.”

Wood, by contrast, is a poor conductor. It resists the flow of heat much more than metal does. So when you touch wood, only a small amount of heat is pulled from your skin at first, and the surface quickly warms up a little. Since your skin loses heat more slowly, the wood feels less cold, even though it is at the same temperature as the metal.

In short, the sensation of cold is not just about temperature; it is about how quickly a material pulls heat out of your body. Metal does that much faster than wood, which is why it feels colder.

That bend you see is caused by **refracted light**.

When light travels from air into water, it changes speed. Since air and water have different densities, the light doesn’t keep moving in the same straight line at the boundary — it bends. That bend is called **refraction**.

With a spoon in a glass of water, the part above the surface is seen through air, but the part below the surface is seen through water. Because the light coming from the underwater portion is bent as it leaves the water and enters the air, your eye interprets it as coming from a slightly different place. The result is that the submerged part of the spoon appears shifted relative to the part above water, which makes the spoon look broken or bent at the surface.

A couple of nice details:

- The effect is strongest when you look at the spoon at an angle, not straight down.
- The deeper the object is in the water, the more noticeable the shift can seem.
- The same principle explains why the bottom of a pool can look shallower than it really is.

So the spoon isn’t actually bending — your brain is being “tricked” by light changing direction as it crosses from water to air. Once you know that refraction is the culprit, the illusion makes a lot more sense.

Those charges allow neighboring water molecules to form hydrogen bonds, which are weak but important attractions between molecules. In liquid water, the molecules move around constantly, breaking and reforming these bonds. As the temperature drops, the molecules slow down and eventually settle into a rigid pattern when water freezes.

The key point is that this frozen pattern is not tightly packed. A spoon looks bent in water because of refraction, which is the bending of light as it passes from one medium into another. When you look at a spoon partially submerged in a glass of water, light reflected from the part below the surface does not travel through water and air in the same way light from the part above the surface does.

Light moves more slowly in water than in air, and this change in speed causes the light rays to change direction at the boundary between the two substances. In other words, when the light leaves the water and enters the air, it bends away from the original path. Your eyes and brain treat light as if it always travels in a straight line, so the shifted rays make the submerged portion of the spoon appear to be in a different place than it really is.

That is why the spoon looks bent or broken right at the waterline, even though the spoon itself is straight. This is a common example of refraction, the same effect that makes a swimming pool appear shallower than it actually is or causes a straw to seem displaced in a drink.

More formally, the amount of bending depends on the angle at which light enters the surface and on the difference in refractive index between air and water. Because water has a higher refractive index than air, the light path changes enough for the illusion to be easy to see. The result is a simple but striking everyday demonstration that light does not always travel along the same path in every material.
